summary:
No trans-specific statute, enforcement series or incident pattern is documented for Yozgat province. That absence records the absence of documented divergence from the national position, not local safety: the rules set out below reach Yozgat unchanged.

Yozgat stands under the national framework of Turkey, where hostility toward LGBTI+ people has hardened into explicit state policy. Kaos GL's 2025 review, "The Year of the Family: A Major Siege Against LGBTI+ People", records "Year of the Family" instructions issued to public institutions and, for the first time in years, the closure of an LGBTI+ rights organisation; expression and artistic freedom were restricted and events cancelled or banned.

The same review counts 313 liberty violations in 2025, roughly two and a half times the previous year, alongside 299 detention decisions. It records 89 torture or ill-treatment violations, up from 51 the prior year, and 61 travel bans. Private-life violations rose from 16 to 67, an increase the review attributes in part to obstruction of trans people's hormone therapy. Six right-to-life violations were documented, three of them hate-motivated killings, with trans people the group most affected.

A draft legislative package would extend that regime into statute. Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked omnibus draft, the "11th Judicial Package", would amend the Turkish penal code to criminalise conduct deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality" with up to three years in prison, and participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with up to four years.

The draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care, including surgery, from 18 to 25, conditioned on mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals. Healthcare professionals performing such interventions would face fines and up to seven years in prison, patients up to three years, with pretrial detention possible.

Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft. Human Rights Watch warns that the measure would force treatment underground and leave LGBT people in constant fear of arrest. Both sources are national-framework material with no provincial breakdown, so neither confirms nor excludes application of these measures within Yozgat.
tangentialFactors:
The 2025 monitoring totals sit alongside a shift in how hostility is expressed: the Kaos GL review frames it as instructions and closures rather than residual prejudice, which means a visitor in Yozgat is entering a jurisdiction where anti-LGBT policy is issued through public administration rather than applied case by case.

The draft package illustrates a gap between text and practice that runs in both directions. It was unpassed when reported, yet the same reporting period produced rising detention and ill-treatment figures, so a pending measure is not a reliable signal of what enforcement on the ground will look like.

The care restrictions in the draft would reshape an existing pathway rather than close one: the age threshold moves from adulthood to 25, and the infertility condition attaches to a legal requirement rather than a medical judgement made by the patient. Travel bans recorded at 61 are a resident-facing sanction, but they share machinery with the checkpoint and document checks a foreign visitor may encounter elsewhere in Turkey.

Yozgat's profile matches the pattern described in the national sources in one specific way: nothing local contradicts them. Provinces without reported incidents appear in the national monitoring for the same reason they appear here, namely that monitoring is organised around detentions, closures and events that concentrate in large cities.

The closure of an LGBTI+ rights organisation and the cancellation or banning of events apply to organising inside the country, as do the "Year of the Family" instructions to public institutions. outOfScopeNotes:
Neither source supplies a provincial breakdown. Whether any of the 313 liberty violations, 299 detention decisions or 61 travel bans recorded in 2025 occurred in Yozgat is not sourced here, and the absence of such reporting should not be read as a finding of no incidents.

The status of the "11th Judicial Package" beyond 29 October 2025 is unresolved in this inventory: whether it was enacted, amended or withdrawn is not stated, and its provisions are described as a leaked draft rather than law.

Whether Yozgat's provincial health authorities issued circulars of the kind reported elsewhere in Turkey, or whether local hospitals apply any of the proposed age and evaluation conditions, is not sourced.

The presence or absence of LGBTI+ organisations, community networks or documented policing practice within Yozgat province is not covered by the inventory, so no local enforcement picture can be stated either way.
